title: Palisades (Holtec restart): External_Sender Holtec Emergency Licensing Amendment Request to The NRC [['E-Mail']]
entity: Heartland Independent Film and Drama Forum

documents.text:
From:      Roger Rapoport
To:        Marlayna Doell
Subject:   [External_Sender] Holtec Emergency Licensing Amendment Request To THe NRC
Date:      Thursday, October 8, 2026 4:09:41 PM



Dear Marlayna Doell and NRC Staff:

Good afternoon.

 I am responding to your short notice request for pubic input
on Holtec International’s request for a one time license
amendment. As you know this request was only noticed on
October 6 in a hard to find Mlive notice followed by NRC
adding it to the website a day later.

Usually there is plenty of time adequate notice for the public
to respond. The applicant’s claim that they are in an
emergency situation is not true.

As a journalist I have done many interviews with people who
have worked at Palisades and other nuclear facilities,
published articles about the plant in the Detroit Free Press, the
Progressive and Counterpunch and produce the Nuclear
Reactor Next Door podcast on Palisades I have spoken to
experts such as the plant’s former design engineering manager
Alan Blind who has already submitted a petition on this mater.

 I appreciate this opportunity to oppose granting an emergency
license amendment.

I want the NRC to deny the emergency license amendment
request and submit this complicated manner to the normal
hearing review process that allows at least 45 days for
 comment, followed by a hearing and NRC review. This has
happened repeatedly in the past with Palisades and needs to
happen again. A departure from the norm is not justified and
could needlessly alarm the public.

Holtec's one of a kind fuel loading failure on August 30, was
not disclosed to the public or the NRC until weeks later.
Obviously there never was or is an emergency. Had this been
the case both the plant owner and the NRC would have said so.
The facts speak for themselves and a ruling in Holtec’s favor
on this application would raise more questions than it answers.

Nothing in Holtec’s application indicates there is any kind of
emergency. In fact emergency license amendments are not
issued in this situation. They are done when an operating plant
has a short term need that makes it prudent to keep the plant in
operation.

As you know emergency license amendments are not granted
for non operating plants. Ruling in Holtec’s favor would set a
dangerous precedent and potentially subject the NRC to
similar emergency applications that are not emergencies. The
net effect of an emergency amendment would be to cut off all
public discussion of how to safely resolve the present
challenges created by the full assembly loading failure.

 By Holtec’s own admission the failed fuel loading on August
30 is not a danger to workers or neighbors. There is also no
threat to the integrity of the plant. The damaged fuel rods can
certainly be stored underwater in the borated pool while Holtec
and the NRC decide what to do next.
 Of course emergencies are situations liked delayed arrival of a
pump for an operating reactor. In that case a licensing
amendments would be justifiable.

Neither Holtec or the NRC have told the public why the
company needs a license amendment related to plant safety.

On the other hand Holtec’s unprecedented attempt to restart
fuel loading requires careful study and discussion with input
from experienced experts like Alan Blind. Failure to carefully
evaluate all points of view could ironically create the kind of “
emergency”that Holtec and the NRC both deny is presently
happening. That would be a bad outcome for all concerned.

In other words Holtec’s plan needs to go through the normal
45 day comment period followed by a public hearing and a
careful analysis that is the heart and soul of the NRC.

 There is one other key point on the radiation exposure limits.
Even if Holtec’s worst case exposure calculation is correct and
falls within legal limits, both workers and the public are
vulnerable.

The fact that this operation can expose a worker to 60 percent
of their annual radiation limit or that vented radioactive gases
are “under”the legal limit does not mean that anyone wants
this to actually happen. In the latter case the amount of
radiation in the gases, albeit “legal" could still trigger an
evacuation order.

There is something else at stake here. Holtec’s rushed plan of
 action could, if it fails, damages the integrity of the company's
plan to reopen the reactor. That would not be in the best
interest of either Holtec or the NRC.

I also want to point out that under the ownership of both
Entergy and Holtec this latest proposal is preceded by a
number of previous events that underscore the concerns
presented in Alan Blind's outstanding petition.

In 1993, a broken fuel rod led to two emergency evacuations
of all plant personnel from the containment, as a precaution
against significant potential radioactive hazards, including
during the recovery operation.

In 2005, a two-day dangle of a 107-ton, fully loaded highly
radioactive waste container above the indoor wet storage pool
was a close call with catastrophe."

From  December 2024 to April 2025, Holtec undertook a
large-scale transfer of highly radioactive waste from the indoor
wet storage pool into outdoor dry cask storage. Holtec did so
with no Radiological Emergency Plan in place, including
evacuation planning for the local, area, and perhaps even
regional population, if a disaster unfolded due to the drop of a
heavy cask into the pool. Holtec took advantage of Palisades'
then decommissioning status, a regulation-free zone, despite
the inherent risks of such an operation.”

None of this is reassuring. I believe it is the best interests of
the public to carefully evaluate Alan Blind’s petition and,
given his experience, have a hearing where he, the NRC and
 Holtec can openly discuss all of his questions. That will be a
benefit to the plant owner, NRC staff and the public.

There is a reason why the NRC has procedures in place to
make sure that the public is part of the opportunity. The
applicant’s claim that there is an emergency is, by its own
admission, false.

I look forward to an opportunity to join a public hearing on
this matter. Please confirm receipt

Sincerely,


Roger Rapoport
